q: 1. The shape of vertical curve generally provided is
explain: Vertical curves connecting two gradients are generally designed as parabolic curves because they provide a constant rate of change of grade and are easy to compute and set out.

q: 2. The 'point of curve' of a simple circular curve is
explain: The point of curve (PC) is where the circular curve begins, i.e., the point of commencement of the curve from the back tangent.

q: 3. Designation of a curve is made by
options: angle subtended by a chord of any length
angle subtended by an arc of specified length
explain: In practice (as per the book's answer key), a curve is designated by its radius, though in many other references degree of curve (angle subtended by a standard chord) is also used.

q: 4. The degree of the curve is the angle subtended by a chord of ... length
explain: In the metric system commonly used in this text, the degree of curve is defined as the angle subtended at the centre by a chord of 25 m (some systems use 30 m for peg intervals; the book's answer key specifies 25 m for degree of curve).

q: 5. An open cross-staff is commonly used for setting out
explain: Since the open cross-staff is a simple, less precise instrument without magnification, it is commonly used only for setting out short offsets where accuracy requirements are modest.

q: 6. Point of tangency is the
options: common point where the radius changes
common point where the radius and direction changes
explain: The point of tangency is where the circular curve ends and merges back into the straight (forward tangent), i.e., the end of the curve.

q: 7. In a simple curve, 'External distance' is the distance between
options: vertex and middle point of the curve
vertex and the centre of the curve
point of curve and point of tangency
explain: External distance is measured from the point of intersection (vertex) of the two tangents to the midpoint of the curve (the midpoint of the arc), along the bisector of the angle of intersection.

q: 8. Let the angular value of one graduation of a tube of length x be theta seconds and R be the radius of its internal curved surface, than
explain: The angular value theta (in seconds) subtended by one division of length x on a bubble tube of radius R is given by theta = x/(206265 R), converting radians to seconds via the constant 206265.

q: 9. The approximate formula for radial or perpendicular offsets from the tangent, is
explain: As per the book's answer key, the approximate offset formula from the tangent to the curve is given as x/R, used for small offsets in curve setting out.

q: 10. Rankine's deflection angle in minutes is obtained by multiplying the length of the chord by
options: square of the degree of the curve
inverse of the degree of the curve
explain: Rankine's method computes the deflection angle (in minutes) for setting out a curve by multiplying the chord length by the degree of the curve, using a simplified tangential angle formula.

q: 11. An ideal transition curve is
explain: The clothoid spiral is considered the theoretically ideal transition curve because its curvature increases exactly linearly with distance along the curve, matching the actual path of a vehicle turning at constant speed.

q: 12. Shift of a curve, is
explain: The shift of a curve (the perpendicular distance the circular curve is shifted inward to accommodate a transition curve) is given by the formula L^2/24R, where L is the transition curve length and R the radius.

q: 13. The spiral angle of a transition curve will be given by the equation
explain: The spiral (deflection) angle of a transition curve at any point is given by the formula phi = L2/(2*R*Ls) which, at the end of a full transition curve of length L, reduces to the standard form L2/2R (for the total spiral length).

q: 14. A simple circular curve is designated by
options: angle subtended at the centre by a chord of any length
angle subtended at the centre by a chord of particular length
explain: A simple circular curve is designated by its degree of curve, which is the angle subtended at the centre by a chord of a specified (particular) standard length.

q: 15. An imaginary line tangent to the longitudinal curve of the bubble tube at its middle points is called
explain: This is the definition of the axis of the level tube - the imaginary line tangent to the bubble tube's curved surface at its centre point.

q: 16. An imaginary line tangential to the longitudinal curve of the bubble tube at its middle point is called
explain: The axis of the level tube (bubble tube axis) is the imaginary line tangential to the curved internal surface of the tube at its centre point.

q: 17. The tangent to the liquid surface in a level tube, is parallel to the axis of the bubble
explain: The tangent to the curved liquid surface of the level tube is parallel to the bubble tube's axis specifically at the mid-point of the bubble.

q: 18. A reverse curve consists of
options: a single curve of a circle connecting two straights
two arcs of different radii bending in the same direction
two arcs of equal radii bending in the same direction
two arcs of equal or different radii bending in the opposite directions
explain: A reverse curve is composed of two circular arcs (of equal or different radii) that curve in opposite directions, joined at a common tangent point.

q: 19. A simple circular curve is designated by the
options: angle subtended at the centre by a chord of any length
angle subtended at the centre by a chord of a particular length
explain: A simple circular curve is conventionally designated by its 'degree of curve', which is the angle subtended at the centre by a chord of one particular standard length (e.g., 30 m or 100 ft).

q: 20. When R is the radius of the curve (in meters), D is the degree of curve (in degrees) and length of the chord is 30 m, then the relation between R and D is
explain: For a 30 m chord definition of degree of curve, the standard relation is R = 1720/D (approximately, derived from R = (chord/2)/sin(D/2) for small D).

q: 21. The angle between the back tangent and forward tangent of a curve is known as
explain: The angle subtended at the centre of the curve between the back tangent and the forward tangent (or equivalently between the two radii to the tangent points) is called the central angle.

q: 22. The angle by which the forward tangent deflects from the back tangent of a curve is called
explain: The deflection angle is, by definition, the angle by which the forward tangent direction deflects from the direction of the back tangent.

q: 23. A deflection angle is
options: more than 90 deg but less than 180 deg
equal to the difference between the angle of intersection and 180 deg
equal to the difference between the angle of intersection and 360 deg
explain: The deflection angle and the angle of intersection are supplementary, so the deflection angle equals 180 deg minus the angle of intersection.

q: 24. The total length of the curve is equal to
explain: The length of a circular curve (arc) subtending an angle phi (in degrees) at the centre, with radius R, is given by L = pi*R*phi/180.

q: 25. Different grades are jointed together by
explain: Vertical curves are used to smoothly join two different longitudinal gradients (grades) on a road or railway alignment.

q: 26. 'Point of curve' is
explain: The 'point of curve' refers to the point of commencement of the curve, i.e., where the curve begins (tangent point at the start).

q: 27. When the curve is to be set out over a rough ground, the method used is
explain: For setting out curves over rough or obstructed ground where linear (chain/tape) methods are impractical, either the two-theodolite method or the tacheometric method can be used, both relying primarily on angular/optical measurement.

q: 28. The angle of intersection of a curve is the angle between
explain: As stated in Q12, the angle of intersection of a curve is the angle between the (prolongation of) back tangent and the forward tangent.

q: 29. The theodolite method of setting out a curve involves
explain: Setting out a curve using a theodolite (with the chord/deflection angle method) requires both linear measurements (chord lengths) and angular measurements (deflection angles).

q: 30. A curve of varying radius is known as
explain: A transition curve is one whose radius varies continuously (from infinity at the tangent point to the design radius at the circular curve), providing a gradual change of curvature.

q: 31. Overturning of vehicles on a curve can be avoided by using
explain: Transition curves gradually introduce curvature (and superelevation) between a straight and a circular curve, reducing the centrifugal effect and thus avoiding sudden overturning tendencies of vehicles.

q: 32. An ideal vertical curve to join two gradients, is
explain: A simple parabolic curve is considered ideal for vertical curves joining two different road/rail gradients, since it provides a constant rate of change of grade.

q: 33. Overturning of vehicles on a curve can be avoided by using
explain: A transition curve gradually introduces superelevation and centrifugal force, preventing sudden lateral forces that could cause vehicles to overturn when entering a circular curve.

q: 34. Setting out of a simple curve by two theodolite method does not require
explain: The two-theodolite method sets out curve points purely by angular intersection from two theodolite stations, without needing any linear (chain/tape) measurements along the curve.

q: 35. In a reverse curve, the super elevation provided at the point of reverse curvature is
options: dependent on the element of reverse curve
explain: At the point of reverse curvature (where the curve changes direction), the superelevation must pass through zero, since the cross-slope needs to reverse from one side to the other.

q: 36. Different grades are joined together by
explain: Two different longitudinal gradients (grades) meeting at a summit or valley are smoothly joined together using a vertical curve.

q: 37. The curve composed of two arcs of different radii having their centers on the opposite side of the curve, is known
explain: A reverse curve consists of two arcs of different (or equal) radii with their centres of curvature on opposite sides of the common tangent point, causing the curve to reverse direction.

q: 38. Perpendicular offset from a tangent to the junction of a transition curve and circular curve equal to
explain: The perpendicular offset from the tangent to the point where the transition curve meets the circular curve is, by definition, equal to the shift of the curve.

q: 39. The properties of autogenous curve for automobiles are given by
explain: The path naturally traced by a vehicle turning at constant speed with uniformly changing steering angle corresponds closely to the properties of the clothoid spiral, making it the ideal transition curve for automobiles.

q: 40. If D is the angle of deflection of a simple curve of radius R, the length of its long chord, is
explain: The long chord of a simple circular curve of radius R subtending a central deflection angle D is given by the standard formula: Long chord = 2R sin(D/2).

q: 41. The chord of a curve less than peg interval, is known as
explain: A chord shorter than the standard peg interval (used typically at the beginning or end of a curve, or where obstructions occur) is called a sub-chord.

q: 42. In Indian tangent clinometer is associated with
explain: As per the book's answer key, the Indian tangent clinometer is associated with chain survey work, used for measuring slope angles in the field alongside chaining.

q: 43. If D is the degree of the curve of radius R, the exact length of its specified chord, is
options: radius of the curve x sine of half the degree
diameter of the curve x sine of half the degree
diameter of the curve x cosine of half the degree
diameter of the curve x tangent of half the degree
explain: The exact chord length corresponding to the degree of curve D is given by the diameter of the curve multiplied by the sine of half the degree of curve (2R sin(D/2)).

q: 44. When the length of a chord is less than the peg interval, it is known as
explain: A chord shorter than the standard peg interval used along the curve is termed a sub-chord.

q: 45. The deflection angle may be directly obtained by setting the instrument to read ... on back station
explain: By setting the theodolite to read 180 degrees while backsighted on the previous station, the forward sighting directly gives the deflection angle without further computation.

q: 46. When R is the radius of the curve (in metres), D is the degree of curve (in degrees) and length of the chord is 30 m, then the relation between R and D is
explain: For a 30 m chord, the standard relation between radius R and degree of curve D is R = 1720/D (approximately, using the chord definition of degree of curve).

q: 47. The angle between the back tangent and forward tangent of a curve (in degrees) and length of the chord is 30 m, then the relation between R and D is
explain: The angle between the back tangent and forward tangent of a curve is, by definition, the central angle (angle subtended at the centre) of the curve.

q: 48. In a lemniscate curve, the angle between the tangent at the end of the polar ray and the tangent at the commencement of the curve (i.e., straight) is ... the angle between the polar ray and the straight
explain: For a lemniscate curve, the angle between the tangent at the end of the polar ray and the initial tangent is exactly double the angle between the polar ray itself and the straight, per the geometric properties of the lemniscate.

q: 49. A reverse curve consists of
options: a single curve of a circle connecting two straights
two arcs of different radii bending in the same direction
two arcs of equal radii bending in the same direction
two arcs of equal or different radii bending in the same direction
explain: A reverse curve is made up of two circular arcs, of equal or different radii, that bend in the same direction relative to their own tangents, reversing overall alignment direction.

q: 50. When the centers of the arcs lie on the opposite sides of the common tangent at the junction of the two curves, it is known as a
explain: When the centres of curvature of two joined circular arcs lie on opposite sides of their common tangent at the junction point, the resulting curve is a reverse curve.
